summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who pays workers hired at the end of the day the same wage as those who worked all day, picturing the generosity of God’s kingdom.
key_insight: The parable is framed by one saying, given in reverse: “many who are first will be last, and the last first” (19:30) and “the last will be first, and the first last” (20:16). It answers Peter’s question, “what shall we have?” Reward in the kingdom rests on the Master’s goodness, not on hours worked.
story: Peter had just asked what the disciples would receive for leaving everything to follow Jesus. Jesus answered with a parable: “For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.” He agreed with them for a denarius a day and sent them to work.

About the third hour he went out again and saw others standing idle in the marketplace. He sent them into the vineyard too, promising, “whatever is right I will give you.” He did the same about the sixth and the ninth hour.
About the eleventh hour he found still others standing there. “Why have you been standing here idle all day?” he asked. “Because no one hired us,” they said. He sent them into the vineyard as well.

When evening came, the owner told his steward to call the laborers and pay them, “beginning with the last to the first.” Those hired at the eleventh hour each received a denarius. When the first came, they expected more, but they too received a denarius each.
They complained against the landowner: “These last men have worked only one hour, and you made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the heat of the day.”

He answered one of them, “Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go your way. I wish to give to this last man the same as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with my own things? Or is your eye evil because I am good?”
“So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few chosen.”

scene.label: The marketplace
scene.text: Day laborers gathered in the village square at dawn and waited to be hired. Most owned no land and lived on what they earned each day. A man still unhired at evening went home with nothing for his family.

scene.label: The hours
scene.text: Hours were counted from sunrise, about 6 a.m. The third hour was about 9, the sixth about noon, the ninth about 3 in the afternoon, and the eleventh about 5, an hour before work ended.

scene.label: Paid at evening
scene.text: The Law required that a hired worker be paid the same day: “Each day you shall give him his wages, and not let the sun go down on it” (Deuteronomy 24:15). The owner keeps the Law exactly.

scene.label: An evil eye
scene.text: In Hebrew speech an evil eye meant envy or stinginess (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22). The owner asks whether his goodness has made them envious.

scene.label: “Many are called”
scene.text: The NKJV includes “For many are called, but few chosen” at verse 16. Some of the oldest manuscripts do not have the words here, though all have them at Matthew 22:14.

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew tells this parable. He places it between Peter’s question about reward (19:27) and Jesus’ third prediction of His death (20:17–19), and wraps it in the saying about the first and the last. In Matthew the King’s generosity, not the length of service, sets the pay.

seeing.reveals: Jesus pictures a Master who goes out again and again to find workers and gives the last what they could never earn. His goodness wrongs no one; it is simply generous.
seeing.living: The complaint is not that anyone was cheated, but that latecomers were treated as equals. If you have served Christ for many years, rejoice when grace reaches newcomers in full measure. If you came late, take your denarius without shame; it was always a gift.
seeing.ponder: When God is generous to someone who seems to have done far less than you, is your eye evil because He is good?

preaching.big_idea: In God’s kingdom the reward is grace: no one is cheated, and latecomers receive in full.
preaching.watch_for: Read it with 19:27–30. Peter asks, “what shall we have?” Jesus promises a rich reward, then tells this parable so that reward will not be counted like wages. The order of payment, last to first, is the hinge (v. 8).
